Mr. Speaker, my first words must be of congratulation to the mover and the seconder of the address; and I want to say that they are spoken on behalf of all those associated with me. I am not able tonight to proceed in the very leisurely fashion adopted by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) this evening; my time is limited and even though I may move an amendment, I shall try to live within my forty minutes.
I am not going to discuss international affairs. The opportunity will come when we may do that. However, I should like to say that I felt it a great privilege to be associated with the delegation which went to the united nations assembly. I want to add that we were happy in the chairman who led our delegation (Mr. St. Laurent).
The Prime Minister and the leader of the opposition have both referred to the several parties, and both have given different reasons why there are more than two parties in this house. I am going to give the correct one. The reason why this party is in the house is that throughout the world over the last half century there has been growing a new philosophy of life, a philosophy based on cooperation and on social ownership, and throughout the civilized world parties which represent that point of view have been gaining strength and gradually assuming power. The struggle today is really between those who believe in social ownership and cooperative endeavour and those who believe in the continuance of the exploitation of the people by powerful groups of vested interests.
I want to say something, too, about the speech from the throne. Apart from expres-
The Address-Mr. Coldwell

sions of self-satisfaction regarding Canada's role in international affairs, the speech from the throne contains only a few vague references to social security, old age pensions and preparations for the next general election; and I say that in this respect it is an unsatisfactory document. Parliament has the right to receive more specific information in order that our electors and the country generally may consider and discuss prospective legislation. Why? In a democracy opportunities must be given for the formation and expression of public opinion by widespread discussion of legislative proposals, in the press, over the radio and in lively discussions among our citizens. Nothing in the speech from the throne discloses the kind of legislation the government intends to introduce; hence no opportunities are provided for the kind of discussion, either in this house or in the country, which may influence or modify in any degree the proposals of the government. I think this is unfortunate, because it comes at a time when democratic institutions and procedures are threatened over wide areas. It indicates, too, that the long term in office of the party opposite has, I think, made it somewhat careless of those great principles upon which this institution of parliament was founded.
Canadians cannot afford to disregard well-established democratic procedures for they are being challenged, as I said a moment ago, all across the world. We must beware lest, in destroying nazi and fascist totalitarianism in a great war, we allow some of the attributes of totalitarianism to corrupt our own institutions. That is why we were alarmed by the methods used to secure the apprehension, inquisition and subsequent prosecution of persons suspected of traitorous conduct last year. We have no sympathy with those who were found guilty of traitorous conduct, but the methods used were not the methods of democracy. That is why my colleague, the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) received in previous sessions of this house the unqualified support of our party in his proposals for a statutory bill of rights safeguarding our citizens against such undemocratic procedures as were used last year. May I add that no matter from what quarter of the house similar proposals are placed before this parliament, we shall be very happy indeed to support them provided that they are sufficiently comprehensive to meet the needs of our time.
But this is a matter which will be fully discussed later in the session. I mention it only to warn the country that Canada is not immune from the dangers to which democratic

procedures are being subjected all across the world. Indeed, the great struggle in which the world is engaged is that of social and economic freedom against forms of dictatorship and serfdom; and this is not a clear-cut, two-way struggle. The lines are blurred. In our politically democratic countries, we have long been subjected to irresponsible controls by powerful economic, and more recently, monopolistic interests. Until these have been brought under social control, freedom, social security and orderly progress will not have been won. Failure to win economic democracy now, which is the aim and goal of democratic socialist parties everywhere, may endanger the very cause for which we fought and deliver us into the hands of a kind of North American fascism, the alternative to which may well be, after upheavals and revolutionary chaos, totalitarian communism. But of course in such a struggle we shall be influenced by world-wide events. Hence it follows that Canadians should do their utmost to support those democratic forces which are struggling for human rights and fundamental freedoms everywhere, and may I add particularly at this time on the continent of Europe. Let us not forget this: though Hitler has been destroyed, political prisons, concentration camps, forced labour, secret police and condemnation without public trial are now normal procedures in many lands. Only in the United Kingdom and in the countries of western Euroupe are the lamps of political freedom in the old world still alight. Thus it seems to me that liberty-loving Canadians should do all in their power to help the European democrats rebuild that war-torn continent on truly democratic principles.
That is one reason we support wholeheartedly Canada's demand for full participation in the peace conferences; for in spite of our lapse into totalitarian methods last year I am certain that Canada's representatives would support the general concept of democratic political principles. But that democratic concept must be firmly established in our own country, and that we have not done; for there can be no real, effective or permanent freedom until our political freedom is complemented with economic freedom. Then, may I say to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) we shall have secured democracy.
We must not confuse democracy with the kind of monopolistic private enterprise we know on this North American continent. The war gave us an opportunity of moving rapidly toward the new freedom which we must achieve. From 1930 to 1939 we had no national plan to secure desirable national objectives. Policies to cope with grave

The Address-Mr. Caldwell
national problems were weak, ineffective, productive of almost hopeless confusion and great distress in our country. Then came the war. Quickly we found that we could not make the required effort by leaving our economy to the profit-seeking motives of the so-called free enterprisers. By conscious planning and direction not only did we provide our armies and our allies with vast quantities of supplies and equipment, but Canadians at home enjoyed on the whole a better standard of living than they had known in recent times.
But what happened? As soon as the war was over, powerful interests began their demands for a return to what they called normal economic relationships. Let me remind this house that these so-called normal economic relationships in 1913 and 1914, as from 1930 to 1939, were unemployment, poverty on our farms, hopeless confusion and widespread distress. Cries for the necessity of respecting some provincial rights which time and evolution have made obsolete, together with demands for what they call voluntary cooperation in the post-war world, have been heard on almost every hand; and the loudest of all come from the lips of the directors of powerful corporations such as our bank presidents, while criticism of public servants, the bureaucrats, as they are called, is promoted by every possible means. But what this means is that public servants planning the production and distribution of essential goods under the scrutiny of parliament shall be replaced by profit-seeking corporation managements responsible to none but their own shareholders, and indeed shareholders who exercise no real authority over them.
Without national planning we revert to economic chaos. Individual industries, with their plants and man-power, interfere with one another and defeat both their own and the public welfare.
The result of these unplanned activities is to reduce living standards and depress wages, which react immediately on farm prices and ultimately prevent many from producing anything at all. Because of the world-wide demand for all kinds of goods, this condition is momentarily obscured by a deceptive prosperity; but sooner than we think we shall need to substitute intelligent planning for the economic anarchy which is the normal rule of what is attractively and deceptively named free enterprise.
Just yesterday I was reading a summary of a bulletin issued last month by the federal reserve bank board at 'Washington. It warns that the United States faces an immediate
economic crisis and that a depression appears unavoidable. It suggests that it may be mitigated by shaving profit margins to the lowest possible levels, and by cutting prices on everything produced for sale. It summarizes the causes as consumer resistance against high prices of goods with which warehouses are jammed; and-
Output of most goods for civilian use has been far in excess of pre-war levels during the past sixteen months, excess inventories of goods have accumulated, and there are likely to be substantial further increases in supplies in coming months.
This, mind you, is from the board of the federal reserve bank. It means that consumer goods have been withheld for higher prices and profits by manufacturers; but because they were all doing it we may all be caught in the trap, for Canada cannot be immune from economic trends in the United States, though by economic planning we could mitigate their evil effects.
I now want to take a look at some of the examples of the government's failure to plan for the benefit of the Canadian people. The housing problem has been mentioned. It is an excellent illustration of the failures of private enterprise. Because private industry found home building unprofitable in the prewar years, there was serious overcrowding at that time. The census returns of both 1931 and 1941 testify to this. But because of delayed marriages, the reestablishment of veterans and arrested construction of homes during the war, the chronic need for housing became particularly acute in the autumn of 1945 and in
1946.	The Prime Minister has quoted certain figures tonight. The Department of Reconstruction and Supply estimated, according to their own statement, an increased requirement of some 80,000 units last year. Government reports indicate-and I will quote the Prime Minister's figure-that 60,000 housing units were completed, so that we began the year with an unsatisfied additional requirement for 1946 of some 20,000 units.
Apart from the heavy export of building material to the United States, we find, according to the government's own figures for the first ten months of 1946, that only S32.38 out of every S100 spent on construction was spent on housing. Tonight the Prime Minister gave a very substantial figure as the amount of construction last year, but when you analyse the figure you find that less than one-third of the amount spent on construction in Canada last year was spent on housing. The building of service stations, hotels, breweries-and you
The Address-Mr. Coldwell

only have to look in this city to find one- Dowling alleys and theatres has gone on while Canadian families lacked shelter.
On November 20 of last year the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe), stated that it was beyond the administrative ability of any group of officials to say what was essential and non-essential housing. Two days later, on November 22, the vice-president of Central Housing and Mortgage Corporation stated:
More houses would be built if construction controls were more effective.
He blamed public opinion for failing to support the postponement of the construction of theatres, bowling alleys and other nonessentials. The minister says the remedy is beyond administrative capacity. Major-General Young says public opinion is at fault. We say it is the failure of the government to give leadership and direction that is to be blamed, and this failure is due to the fact that the government will not control, does not believe in controlling, private interests who can make more money by exporting lumber to the United States or by building a brewery' or a theatre than by building homes for the people.
The minister's excuses cannot be accepted. When we were at war-and to his credit be it said-he found experts who could decide what was essential and what was non-essential. The war needs overrode the production for profit principle. Now the needs of national health, the reduction of juvenile delinquency, fire prevention and the conservation of human life demand that the means we found to be effective to win the war against Hitler shall be applied to preserve and improve the health, living and moral condition of our people. We all recall the regrettable fire in this city only a week ago following which the fire chief remarked that had there been proper housing facilities the deaths would probably not have occurred.
But the government does not heed the desires or necessities when put before it by parliament itself. According to its own departs mental food pronouncements, for example, a child should consume one quart of milk a day, or thirty quarts a month. In order to encourage this desirable consumption the house on August 27 last passed as strongly worded a motion as our rules permit requesting the continuance of the consumers' milk subsidy. But the government flouted the obvious desire of parliament by' removing this subsidy in October. One is constrained to inquire how the Prime Minister forgot his oft-repeated statement that of course parliament must decide. Milk increased by three cents a quart in most cities, so that the cost of milk per child rose 
by ninety cents a month. Of course children of parents in the lower income groups bought less milk. Instead of taking steps to encourage production and increased consumption, the government has taken effective steps to reduce both.
Nor must we forget this: the increased milk prices account, with other government policies, for the steady increases in the cost of living this winter; and these increases will be reflected before long in lessened demand for goods and increased demands for higher wages, and the upward adjustments of prices of commodities produced on our farms. And these demands will be legitimate and entirely proper.
Within the last few days the government has lifted certain price ceilings, one result of which is that shortening goes up by ten cents a pound. The price of soap-yes, soap, to the advertising of which we have to listen hour after hour on the radio, when millions of dollars are spent for advertising-has been permitted to increase. The cost of clothing is allowed to go up. Those of us who have been buying clothing-shirts, and the like- know perfectly well that the price is already high and the quality very much poorer than before the war.
Let us for a moment look at the farm situation. Long ago the government announced that the price of food would be one of the last to be released from pripe control. Lately ceilings have had to be raised. But the government maintains farm ceilings, raising them only after other prices have risen sharply. This means that prices of farm products always lag behind farmers' costs of production. While holding the line on living costs, of which food is a major item, is undoubtedly sound national policy the government has no right to inflict the burden of its costs upon the farmer, the producer. Yet that is the effect of the government policy of lifting the price ceiling from commodities which the farmer must buy and retaining them as long as the government dares on things he must sell. Thus the farmer is made to subsidize the consumer.
I might illustrate this by reference to the wheat industry. As we all know, the price of wheat to the United Kingdom under the wheat agreement is SI.55 a bushel basis Fort William. But wheat used for Canadian consumption on the same basis is available to Canadian millers at SI.35 a bushel. This means that the farmer, not the government, is subsidizing our bread to the extent of twenty cents a bushel of wheat.
Of course this is in addition to a milling subsidy of fifty-seven cents from the public

The Address-Mr. Coldwell
treasury, to which the farmer must also contribute. The milling industry, I believe, gets its wheat for milling purposes at about seventy eight cents a bushel. I am not suggesting that bread should not be subsidized, but I am saying that the national budget and not the Canadian farmer should bear the charges that flow from it.
The long-term outlook for agriculture is also vital to Canada's economic and social progress, as well as to the general welfare of mankind. The farmers need long-term agreements for wheat, dairy produce, hogs, poultry, eggs, fruit and so on. And to the extent that they have been made, steps have been taken in the right direction.
When making these agreements we need to establish what parity prices are. Let me point out that parity prices-and I remind my hon. friends to the right of this-demand comprehensive national planning and controls. You cannot maintain parity without them. What do we mean by parity? I believe I should say what we mean. We mean the establishment of a proper relationship between prices of commodities which the farmer must buy and prices of the produce he must sell. Obviously there can be no such parity when the producer is left to the tender mercies of speculative markets.
Mr. LaGuardia appeared before the United Nations Organization. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) was there, as was the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). I, too, was there; and we all heard him. At these recent meetings of the United Nations Assembly Mr. LaGuardia underlined the statement I have just made when he said:
"You cannot have both stability in prices and security for the farmer as well as fluctuation in prices.^ It is no use saying that we are not going to interfere with free exchange and free sales. If you want what is needed," Mr. LaGuardia warned, "you will interfere, and you will put every gambling grain exchange out of business in Chicago, Winnipeg, in Liverpool or wherever it exists."
I noticed that in the course of the many speeches which followed his forthright statements, of which this is but a sample-and some of his other statements were equally forthright-no delegate from any of the fifty-four nations including Canada sitting around that table expressed any disagreement with Mr. LaGuardia's statement.
What I have said with respect to farm returns lagging behind price increases applies equally to labour. Wages and salaries have remained constant to a large extent, although there have been increases in some fields while 83166-6
others have decreased. For example-and I take this information from the Labour Gazette -the average weekly wages in manufacturing industries dropped from $30.71 in 1945 to $29.53 in 1946. On the other hand the cost of living index rose from 119-5 to 127-1 in the same period, an increase of more than six per cent. This, I would add, fell heavily on old age pensioners, pensioners from the last war, people living on government annuities, and others with small fixed incomes. Thus every dollar the wage-earner or pensioner received bought less than ninety-four cents worth of necessities in 1946 compared with 1945. Indeed since the war ended the purchasing power of Canadian industrial workers in Canadian dollars has dropped to ninety cents. This is due to the failure of the government to hold the price line, and accounts for the unrest which is growing in the industrial and rural areas. Because of all this I move an amendment to the amendment:
That the following words be inserted in the amendment, after the word "motion" and before the word "we";
"We respectfully submit, however, that in the opinion of this house Your Excellency's advisers have shown a readiness to return to the policies of uncontrolled and unplanned private enterprise which resulted in the depression and unemployment of pre-war years;
And further that Your Excellency's adivsers have failed to introduce comprehensive measures for the socialization of the financial institutions and monopolistic industries of the country, and thus have failed to plan the full and proper use of our natural resources and our currency and credit in such a way as to provide for full production and a rising standard of living for the Canadian people;
Therefore in their failure to recognize these basic needs we respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's present advisers do not possess the confidence of the country."
But there is a limited group in our Canadian economy which has not suffered. According to the Bank of Canada statistics summary for November, 709 of Canada's largest corporations received $273 million in profits after all taxes had been paid. This was $3 million more than in the previous year. But according to the Financial Post, December 28, 1946, 28 large Canadian companies actually showed net profits after taxes of $52,000,000, an increase in profits last year of over 55 per cent. I quoted these figures and their source on the air on January 22, and the Financial Post commented editorially on what I had said. They wrote:
In his national radio speech last week, CCF Leader Coldwell used the familiar tactics of his party in quoting partial figures and comparing non-comparable items, in order to build up a totally false impression. He said:

The Address-Mr. Coldwell

"During the past year, average weekly earnings of industrial workers rose from $32.16 to $33.23-a rise of less than 4 per cent. Over the same period, the profits, after taxes, of 28 of Canada's largest corporations, rose from $33 millions to $52 millions, a rise of 56 per cent."
Then the Financial Post went on to say that that was not a fair comparison because all of this increased amount earned by the corporations after taxes had not been distributed in dividends, that part of it had been used for capital accumulations. I should like to know why money which has been obtained in profits and is kept by a corporation for the expansion of that corporation does not belong to the shareholders of the corporation and should not be considered in their profits. I think their figures and my deductions from them are correct.
And if we look at the nine large chartered banks we see their profits during the past year ranged all the way from 9-5 per cent to 19-9 per cent on their paid-up capital. This again underlines the necessity for socializing the chartered banks and controlling our currency and credit issues in terms of public need as the Prime Minister suggested in Edmonton during the election campaign in 1935. Yet powerful corporations and institutions demand the elimination of public controls and the drastic reduction of taxes on business profits.
The C. C. F. does not urge the retention of controls for controls sake, but we do demand that where controls are necessary for the welfare of our people they shall be continued. As for taxes, let us relieve those in the lower brackets and continue to get as much revenue as possible from those who can afford to pay.
I have, I believe, said sufficient to prove that the government's economic policies are not in the best interests of the masses of the people of this country. For a time the deceptive prosperity of this post-war period, caused by unusual demands due to war shortages at home and abroad and accumulated war savings. will lull many into a sense of false security. But the time will come when we shall regret the return of our economy to the private monopolies and enterprises whose policies led us to disaster after the first great war. This time machines are more efficient, man-power more productive and the world less able to buy our surpluses than in the nineteen-twenties.
Even if the world succeeds in clearing channels of trade our prosperity will still depend upon our ability and willingness to plan our economic life to meet our own needs and the needs of mankind. Indeed the welfare of the world in the final analysis will depend upon

the intelligence of individual nations to plan and play their proper parts. It is because Canada is looking back to former ways and policies that we wish to record our lack of confidence in the government's economic policies.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, I trust that I shall be able to follow the very commendable example of the mover of the resolution (Mr. MacNaught) which we are now debating and make my contribution to the debate brief. If I am to do this I will not be able to spend time on the pleasantries usual on such occasions; rather I propose to get right down to work. I do not intend to spend much time either on the speeches which have been made by the other leaders. I should like to assure the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on behalf of this group that we are prepared to get into the business of this session swiftly and to expedite the business of this house as we have always been ready to do, and to honour our agreements when they are made. This is one group in the House of Commons that has always kept its pledge to the Prime Minister and to other leaders when it came to adopting measures to expedite the business of the house.
I should like to mention one thing that arose out of the Prime Minister's speech. I cannot speak for any other group on this side of the house; I would not want to; but I certainly can say in answer to the Prime Minister's statement that no group on this side is prepared to form a government, that here is one group that is not in this House of Commons with the major purpose of attaining political power. Here is one group that is quite ready to cooperate with any other party here that will set out to do the job which the people of this country are demanding. But I assure the Prime Minister that if the other groups or some other group of this house do not start some real action toward implementing the desires of the people, then naturally we are going to set out to do it ourselves. I believe we have thus far given pretty fair evidence of our ability to organize the people and to get them to speak with one voice. Of course I do not need to mention Pontiac, nor do I need to mention the fine showing that we made in the Richelieu-Vercheres by-election where, within a period of less than a year and a half, we were able to bring up our following, our ballot and support, from about 900 to well over 6,000.
Let me say right here, sir, that I welcome into this house another young supporter of this movement, the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Caouette) and to assure him that the voice of Quebec will now be prominent

The Address-Mr. Low
amongst us, and it will be one more reason why the Prime Minister will have to give increasing attention to this great movement, the Social Credit movement.
Thus far we have been neglected; we have been relegated to the ranks of the nobodies; we have not been considered as a national movement; but I wish to point out that within a few months, a veiy few years at the most, the Prime Minister is going to have to recognize us as a great national movement that is determined to establish in Canada a free Christian democracy.

speechtext:
Some of the Prime Minister's
own followers seem to have very short sight, and it is difficult for them to understand.
Just one word about the speech of the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell). I cannot agree in any way with his statement with respect to the great world struggle. Actually I think it must be apparent to any student of world affairs that the great struggle in the world today is between those who seek to extend individual personal freedom and free moral agency on the one hand, and the forces which advocate compulsion and regimentation on the other. I do not apologize for one moment for classing myself amongst the former. Furthermore I say to you, sir, that it is my belief and the belief of those in this group in the l ouse, that any time the government sets out to achieve as its major conscious objective full employment, social security, or a planned economy, that government is going straight down the road to slavery of the people in the country. In his day the Master said:	"Seek ye first the
kingdom of God and His righteousness and all else shall be added unto you." I imagine that if He were here today looking at things through the eyes of a mortal individual, as He once did, He doubtless would say to the people of this country and to the world in general: Seek with all your might to preserve your 83166-61
free moral agency and extend your individual personal freedom to the utmost possible limit, without interfering with the same rights of others, and all these other things will come as a natural consequence.
Since we last met and debated the over-all government policy as revealed in the speech from the throne the great north land of Canada has come more and more into the spotlight of world attention. Spectacular advances and improvements in 1he communication and transportation facilities throughout the world have brought home to thinking people everywhere the very few short hours of flying time between any two points on the earth. If one examines a global map he is struck with the fact that Canada's north land now holds the most important position on the crossroads of international airlines between the three continents, North America, Europe and Asia. This alone gives the north of Canada tremendous strategic importance. But when the economic possibilities of this vast area in our north are brought into sharp focus against the background of its strategic importance it is only then that we realize or begin to realize that a mere twelve million Canadians face a challenge at least comparable with any challenge that Canadians have ever faced in their history. Whether we meet that challenge successfully and well might, in my opinion, be a major factor in future peace or international devastation.
Everyone knows of the gold, silver and copper and many other minerals of undreamed-of value in the pre-Cambrian shield. In the past few years I believe many Canadians have seen for themselves the vast resources of timber, fur, fish and game to be found in the north. A limited number know about the agricultural possibilities for thousands of farm settlers in a number of different sections in that great region. The discovery of one of the world's few sources of uranium accentuated the strategic, as well as the economic importance of the area around Great Boar lake; and only just recently, as some hon. members may have heard, tantalum has been found in some quantity in the territory just north of Alberta. Already there is being constructed at Edmonton a processing plant for this very precious mineral, the production of which will be used for making steel to withstand the terrific pressures and temperatures in the building of rocket planes or jet-propelled weapons and planes. Our uranium, tantalum and oil deposits in the Yellowknife, Great Bear lake and Fort Norman districts are closer to Russia than they are to Toronto, which fact may give
The Address-Mr. Low

/6
some emphasis to what I should like to say now about the north. Canada must get a move on and develop that great territory.
I was very much disappointed that the speech from the throne made no mention of the government's intention to enter upon a bold, progressive and systematic programme of development in the north, and its colonization as well. I know that the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. Glen) is much concerned about the matter. I compliment him warmly upon the things that he has already done in that direction during his short term of office. He has given evidence of a knowledge about the north and its incalculable values not only to Canada but to America as a whole. I only wish that his concern was shared by more members of the cabinet. For joining with the Alberta government in building the Grimshaw-Slave lake highway I want personally to thank the Minister of Mines and Resources. That one artery of transportation will undoubtedly thrust far northward the area of settlement, agriculture, mineral, lumbering and fishing production. But transport and communication facilities are lagging far behind in that vast north country. The government must come to realize that the building of means of transport and communication comes first in any worth-while programme of northern development. The Minister of Transport, I suggest, will have to put the bee on the railways and needle them along into a building programme down there so that settlement and development can proceed with dispatch to meet the challenge facing Canada in a world of crowded countries whose people are looking with astonishment at twelve million Canadians trying to hold on to and spread themselves over three and a half million square miles of territory.
Let me mention that the Alberta government has sensed the tremendous importance of the north. With their limited means in the past few years they have extended a network of roads into the farthest part of the Peace River country, which is the gateway into that north land. They have pioneered winter roads and survey's into territories beyond their boundaries in the north. Telephone lines they have built to serve the growing population in that country, and recently long distance telephone connections have been secured from the northern and western Peace River towns with the outside centres; but these need to be improved and extended.
Among their concrete achievements the Alberta government has recently' commenced a vast scheme of clearing and colonization of lands in the Peace River country which in
rMr. Low.]
five years' time will result in 200,000 acres of new farms being brought under cultivation and production. The government there arranges to clear and break the land and to get it ready' for cropping. Roads are built in to the new farms to make them accessible and veterans of world war II are given a half-section on terms that are at once the finest and the most commendable that I have heard of anywhere.
In ten y'ears' time these men will have title to these farms and there will be no spectacle of Canadian heroes carrying, in twenty years, burdens of unpayable debt such as are still owed by heroes of world war I. Under the stimulus of this new and orderly colonization and settlement the Peace River will become a much greater producer of grains and live stock for which she is already world famous, and she will also become the greatest seed producing area in the world. Grey wooded soils up there, together with the climate, make possible a tremendous production of alfalfa, alsike, and sweet clover seed, eagerly' sought for by the seed houses of the world.
I mention this to give some idea of the growing importance of the northland, which includes the Peace River; and second, to accent the imperative need for a carefully conceived and properly-integrated programme of transport and communication development for the Canadian north, a matter in which in my opinion this government must be prepared to take the lead. With these facilities settlement and development will follow quickly and the north land will become a source of great strength and comfort to all America and not Canada alone.
Let me mention another matter which in my humble judgment will affect our country, favourably or adversely as the case may be, for many years to come. I refer to what has already been discussed by other speakers, namely, the matter of dominion-provincial relations. The speech from the throne makes reference to negotiations that have been carried on for tax agreements with the provinces, over the past number of months. To the average onlooker these negotiations have had more the appearance of a poker game or a juggling exhibition. It is not my purpose to place or even to attempt to place, the blame for what has gone on, but it is a disgraceful state of affairs in Canada when individual provinces find it necessary to protect themselves in the course of negotiations by a most-favoured province clause. That one thing itself indicates that the federal government had no clear-cut idea as to where it was

The Address-Mr. Low
going when, in an effort to bolster up an outworn financial policy, it started to arrogate to itself the most lucrative, I should say, of the remaining provincial tax fields.
It must be obvious that there is yet no properly calculated formula by which rental values can be placed on taxes that are to be surrendered temporarily to the senior government. That the negotiations thus far have seriously impaired Canadian unity is, I think, beyond any question. Every one of us must realize that the difficult years ahead will demand the greatest possible measure of unity among our peoples and governments if Canada is to face squarely and successfully the serious challenge that threatens our very survival as a nation; and it is because I believe that sincerely, and in no sense because I wish to be destructively critical, that I throw out these suggestions.
Let me make it abundantly plain that it is not a question of lecturing the government on what they should do. I merely state what I think are the criticisms of the government's policy, and I am not afraid to stand up and say what I would do if I were in the government's place. In the first place, the government must realize that any agreement covering rental of tax fields from the provinces is only a transitional or interim agreement and not in any sense a permanent solution of the problems of dominion-provincial relations. That the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) partly realizes this is evidenced by the fact that the agreements are to be signed for a period of five years and that another conference is to be held one year ahead of the termination of the contracts.
In the second place, it must be driven deeply into the consciousness of all governments in Canada that nothing in the proposed agreements apparently touches on a permanent solution of the two most important problems affecting the relations of the dominion and the provinces, which are these:	We must soon
clarify and redefine the respective responsibilities of the dominion and the provincial governments. It seems imperative that specific statements of the rights of individual citizens of Canada be drawn perhaps through a bill of rights such as I suggested last session, together with a detailed delineation of the responsibilities attaching to these rights, which each government is prepared fully to assume.
Then the senior government must allocate to the provinces sufficient revenues to enable them fully to discharge their responsibilities at all times. The federal government need not lack for money. They are limited in that respect only by the combined total production
of all the people of Canada. We ought to have learned a lesson from the hungry thirties. At that time the burden of providing social services for the people was heavy on the provincial governments and they found themselves without the means of furnishing those services. Serious results have followed which in some provinces may not be entirely overcome for many years.
I think it is clear to most students of the subject that the interpretations which have been placed on some sections of the British North America Act by the courts have had the effect of handing serious and heavy responsibilities to the provinces and at the same time denying them the means whereby they could do the jobs that have been expected of them.	,
Millions of Canadians today are demanding a rewriting of the constitution so as to clarify the rights of citizens, to define and divide the fields of responsibilities of the governments, to decentralize and give more power to the provinces-not less-and to allocate to the governments, dominion and provincial, the means of discharging fully their respective obligations. I believe that no Canadian unity and solid strength will be possible until this is done, but let it be done 'properly. Rewriting the constitution should not be delegated to a royal commission or a series of royal commissions. It should be accomplished at government level. The machinery of the dominion-provincial conference, in my opinion-the machinery already in existence with some real achievements to its credit-could be used to lay the foundations for the rewriting of the constitution. I suggest that this machinery be made permanent, .perhaps attached to a new department of dominion-provincial relations, and that it be set in motion now to work out proposals for permanent solution of dominion-provincial problems, these to be placed before a conference or a series of conferences during the years immediately ahead. We should not wait until four years from now, just a year before the termination of the tax contracts that are about to be entered into, to try to find permanent solutions. I say that now is the time to begin to develop these fair and equitable scientific formulae for the distribution of powers and the allocation of revenues which we must have if governments in this country are to do their jobs as they should, and if Canadian unity is to be brought to the high level for which we all pray. The social credit movement of Canada is committed to the rewriting of the constitution along these lines, decentralized lines. We demand of the government that it be undertaken at the earliest possible time.
The Address-Mr. Low

I have noticed, Mr. Speaker, that external affairs occupy a very large part of the speech from, the throne. I am not in a position intelligently to discuss the part which Canada has played in the united nations organizations, for to this date the Prime Minister has not seen fit to invite anyone from my organization to attend as a delegate .at any one of them. Therefore I must speak as an onlooker and not as a participant. One wonders if the government is not over emphasizing external relations in some respects to the neglect of pressing internal matters. I am prepared to grant that Canada must assume her full place and responsibility in the world community of nations, and to contribute her utmost to the achievement of world peace and security. At the same time it is obvious to me that we cannot hope to exert any substantial influence for peace in the world unless Canada is strong and unless her people are happy and united. Setting our own house in good order must precede any attempt to try to tell other nations how they .should keep their houses. We have a real job of house-cleaning to do right here at home and I suggest that it should not be neglected. I do not in any way minimize the importance of a strong, nonpartisan foreign policy for Canada, but I do say that the very essence of strong, independent and sovereign nations within the British commonwealth rests in complete understanding and the fullest possible cooperation with each other on foreign policy. Canada, we cannot help noting, failed to support Britain on the Jewish problem in Palestine. Why? Britain in turn failed to support Canada when she accepted Zaroubin as Soviet ambassador to that country after he had violated the recognized code of diplomatic relations right here in Canada. This government, the Liberal government, demonstrated lamentable weakness when it did not protest vigorously against the acceptance by Britain of this man, Zaroubin. We took a slap in the face. How can one explain such extraordinary surrender to fear or inertia? Could it be the result of socialist influence in Canada?
There can be no strength and no vitality in Canada if they are continuously sapped by enemies and leeches from within. It must be evident to the least observant amongst us that the Liberal government has failed to provide adequate safeguards against the perfidy of the enemies within our gates. There was a time, I submit, when the great Royal Canadian Mounted Police force was more than a match 'or any of those who would

betray Canada into the hands of foreign powers or disrupt and destroy us internally. The force would still be capable of coping with the dangers had not government policy made conditions within the force so unattractive, particularly in the special investigations branch, that many of the best men have been drained off entirely, or have gone into ordinary constabulary work.
The failure of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to deal with the rising menace to security in Canada during the war years, which culminated in the recent espionage fiasco, was not due to lack of knowledge of what was going on. Their investigators filed numerous reports with the authorities as far back as 1943 and 1944, showing in detail exactly what the traitors were hatching and what dangers we faced. There is some evidence to show that these reports were pigeonholed and forgotten, and that some investigators were told in effect to leave that sort of thing alone. In the meantime the disrupters continued to go about their nefarious subversive work unchallenged; and had it not been for Gouzenko and his revelations they would likely still be furnishing foreign countries with our secrets. Indeed, news reports this very day would indicate that there may yet be traitors in high places in our country. As the situation now stands, subversive elements in Canada are still making ready for the communist world revolution that has been projected for a number of years.
In the name of millions of Canadians who sense the danger I demand that the government at once make conditions much more attractive in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police force so as to encourage into the service the best men Canada has for that work, and at the same time to develop a strong special investigations branch of the force, untrammeled and free to investigate and report on anyone regardless of his station, against whom there is evidence of treasonable or unlawful subversive activities. If we are to check the spread of treason and disruption, amongst other measures the government will have to take, they will have to do two things. They will have to revitalize our democracy so that it may succeed in removing reasons for discontent among our people, and they will have to issue orders to officers of the police force to take off their gloves and go to work when reports come in showing dangerous conditions or conditions which may become dangerous. At the same time, Mr. Speaker, let us make absolutely sure that the rights and the liberties of our people are safeguarded in every possible

The Address-Mr. Low
way, but let us clean house right now before Canada surrenders to communism and its fellow-travellers.
As an aid to this revitalized special investigations branch of the force I propose that this House of Commons set up a continuing watchdog committee on subversive activities similar to the Dies committee in the United States. The personnel of this committee should be satisfactory to the whole house, chosen much as select standing committees are now chosen. The government, in my estimation, could not be trusted to select such an important committee ; their inability to choose advisers other than those who have led this country by the nose through socialist policies to a virtual socialist state would indicate that parliament must itself set up the committee and lay down its duties. The people of Canada will expect an answer to these proposals; for most Canadians are awakening to the dangers which beset us from within as well as from without, and they want vigorous and effective action to make Canada secure. Let me give this warning:	only when our own people in
Canada are at peace amongst themselves, and free from the influence of subversive, disrupting forces can we ever hope to contribute effectively to the achievement of world peace and security, which is our aim in international affairs.
In setting our house in order the government must not overlook the two most vexatious impediments to large-scale production in Canada. I refer to punitive taxation and continued rigid controls. In spite of statements to the contrary by at least one member of the government, producers all over Canada have assured me during the past six months that high taxation does continue to discourage production of many lines of wanted goods and foodstuffs. Somehow the government does not seem to understand that we can never meet with success the threat of inflation unless the floodgates of production are opened wide, and unless every serious discouragement to large-scale production is removed.
The present high level of taxation is unnecessary. The people of Canada are beginning to understand that this is so and are mobilizing vast movements from one end of the country to the other to win from this government a progressively diminishing tax load. Failing this, they will put into office a government that will bow to the will of the people and do what they are told. It should be noted that an already serious shortage of teachers and nurses in this country has been aggravated by the action of the government last session in lowering exemptions on incomes
earned by married women. In my judgment that action was premature. This group will continue to fight for a substantial reduction in the tax load upon the people, and that beginning immediately.
As to controls, we will not be prepared to grant any blanket controls to the government under the terms of legislation proposed in the speech from the throne. Any specific controls the government is able to convince us beyond any reasonable doubt they need to protect the welfare of the Canadian people as a whole, will receive our support. All the others must go, as far as we are concerned.
There is one other matter about which I should like to speak briefly before I close. Lately the world has been witnessing some most shocking demonstrations of organized interference with free elections in various countries, particularly those where communist influence has grown strong. Scandalous intimidation, brutality, disfranchisement and irregularities of all kinds have become the usual order in elections in Poland and certain other countries. That is bad enough in Europe; I say it would be terrible in Canada. I see some hon. members of the house beginning to shift a bit uneasily in their seats for fear I might be leading up to Richelieu-Vercheres. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what I am leading up to. Decent Canadians were appalled at what went on there during the contest which closed on December 23. Intimidation, brutality, and organized gangsterism raised their ugly heads, especially at Sorel in Richelieu-Vercheres county. What went on at Sorel puts at least one Canadian election in the same class as those carried on in Poland. There was theft of electoral lists and lists of poll workers of one of the parties in the contest. There was dictatorship and intimidation of voters by employers who told their men, "If you don't vote Liberal you may have to eat crusts after the election." There was dereliction of duty on the part of the police, municipal and provincial authorities. There was certainly brutality and hoodlumism by a group of hired gangsters.
The finger of suspicion points directly at the Liberal party as the instigators of the whole dastardly demonstration. That is why I expected the Prime Minister would be quick to ask for a thorough investigation. I still say he owes it to his party to clear them of this suspicion or to condemn their actions if investigation shows that the Liberal organization or any part of it is guilty. The Prime Minister's silence condoned all that went on at Sorel; and decent people all over Canada feel
so
The Address-Mr. Low

that he owed it to them and this country to issue an immediate statement condemning in the strongest possible terms the appearance in a Canadian election of practices now all too common wherever the communists have a considerable hand. But for some unaccountable reason he kept silent.
It must be a source of great sorrow to the Prime Minister to behold the certain decadence of the Liberal party and the things to which some parts of that organization will stoop in order to win an election. Of course one can understand quite well why the Prime Minister did not want another Pontiac, and why he issued instructions to his organization down in Quebec that there must not be another Pontiac; but Richelieu-Vercheres was an extremely hollow victory for the Liberals. In the name of decent people everywhere I condemn the irregularities and the gangsterism which took place in Sorel. That sort of thing must not be allowed to interfere with free elections in Canada, and we must be quick to stamp it out before it becomes an established practice and habit.
All this could have been avoided, I contend, if the government had not been asleep, or if the Liberal party had not surrendered to communist tactics supported by the influence of individuals who could speak with the voice of money. It would appear to a great many people that the time has passed when it is any longer safe for the people to allow their political parties to keep hidden the sources of their funds, because it is by the use of substantial funds that such things as happened at Sorel can be caused to happen. The people should demand that legislation be enacted forthwith in this house to provide that every political party shall have to account for the sources of their finances. To illustrate, the people back home in Alberta, where they look at things quite realistically, have wondered how a comparatively minor group, the C.C.F., for example, by the mere acquisition of David Lewis and a trip to New York by their leader, could suddenly flood the country with organizers and propaganda, and in these things outdo the parties whom the C.C.F. had hitherto ridiculed for doing the same thing.

Mr. LOW; If the C.C.F. have nothing to hide I suggest that they join with us in making this demand. I feel sure the government party, too, will be only too glad to set at rest the talk one hears in various parts of the

country that the rising financial fortunes of the Liberal party are the result of fat war contracts.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the house for the very courteous hearing it has given me during these thirty minutes. I assure hon. members that if they would like to go into some of these matters a little more fully in caucus tomorrow morning, I shall be here to help them.
